newsitem.title: UK: More delay seen over BA /American alliance.
newsitem.headline: More delay seen over BA /American alliance.

text.p: British trade minister Ian Lang has postponed an announcement on whether he is going to block British Airways' proposed alliance with American Airlines until at least next month, industry sources said on Friday.
The industry believes Lang is holding back to try to avoid a potential clash with the European Commission (EC), which is conducting its own investigation into the controversial deal.

"The key problem is who has the right to vet this (deal)," said one source. "What they are probably anxious to avoid is some kind of row where the Commission comes to one decision and the UK comes to another."
The British Department of Trade and Industry declined to comment on when Lang might make his ruling and said he did not have to wait first for the results of any EC investigation.

But a government official later said: "The situation is that the EC and the UK are conducting parallel investigations under Articles 89 and 88 respectively of the Treaty of Rome and in doing so we are cooperating closely and exchanging views on analysis in order to try and avoid a difference in outcome."

However, the EC has already said the results of its wider ranging review into a series of airline alliance are not expected before next March. This has prompted speculation that a showdown between Britain and the EC over which has final say over the alliance may prove unavoidable.

Lang has been due to make a ruling since he received the results on September 17 of an investigation by the Office of Fair Trading (OFT) into the proposed BA/American alliance under which the two airlines would pool their transatlantic routes through a code-sharing arrangement.
Britain and the United States are due to resume related "open skies" trade talks next month aimed at freeing up competition on transatlantic routes.
"I can't believe he can put off a decision until next March one industry source said.
Lang declared in July that Britain would examine the proposed alliance not only under British competition rules but also under the authority of Article 88 of the Treaty of Rome.

The move followed an announcement by the Commission that month that it was launching its own investigation into both the BA and American deal and five other transatlantic airline alliances under Article 89.

Article 88 provides for Member States of the EU to check commercial agreements for compliance with EU competition law whereas Article 89 provides for investigation by the Commission and for enforcement "in cooperation with Member States."
The UK government subsequently said it regarded the Commission investigation as subsidiary to the work of the British competition authorities.
But which article has precedence in reality remains to be seen. "It is an untested area. There are no precedents," said a political source on Friday.
